title: Sky documents inbound payment instructions in its constitution because there is no accounts-receivable function to correct mistakes
content:
A.4.6 opens an Article whose stated subject is administrative plumbing: it "defines maintenance or housekeeping mechanisms and contracts used to administer the Sky Ecosystem," and A.4.6.1 narrows to "standard procedures for sending tokens to Sky." A.4.6.1.1 is titled for the residual case — the process for returning tokens "when no specific process exists."

It is worth asking why a constitutional document contains a payment address. In a conventional organization, a misdirected payment is fixed by a finance team: they identify it, reverse it, or credit it manually, and the instructions themselves are informal because errors are recoverable.

On-chain, none of that holds. There is no counterparty who can reverse a transfer, no discretion to credit a payment that the ledger did not record, and — as the DssBlow2 provisions make explicit — no recovery for an asset sent somewhere that cannot process it. The instructions *are* the mechanism. Publishing them in the Atlas gives them a single authoritative location, makes them changeable only through governance, and creates a citable rule for the follow-on question of who bears the loss when they are not followed.

The design lesson generalizes beyond Sky: in systems where operations are irreversible, operational documentation must be treated as normative rather than as a wiki page. The presence of a catch-all "no specific process exists" default is the other half of the same insight — unanticipated inbound value will arrive, and a system without a defined default acquires stranded assets and undischarged obligations by accident.
description: A.4.6 elevates "maintenance or housekeeping mechanisms" to a governed Article, publishing named contracts and per-asset routing as normative rules rather than leaving them to operator convention.
